newsitem.title: USA: Coffee, palladium prices plummet, soybeans jump.
newsitem.headline: Coffee, palladium prices plummet, soybeans jump.

text.p: Coffee prices plummeted on Friday as profit-taking by nervous speculators ahead of the weekend took some of the air out of the most spectacular bubble in the coffee market in two decades.
At the Coffee Sugar and Cocoa Exchange in New York, coffee for July delivery fell 38.40 cents a pound to close at 276.40, a decline of 12 percent in one day.

Selling of futures by speculators to cash in profits from a three-day rally this week accelerated late in the day. But the July coffee contract still posted a net gain of 20 cents a pound for the week, and coffee prices remain at the highest levels since June 1977.
"It's foolish to think a market goes in only one direction," said Merrill Lynch analyst Judith Ganes. "When it rises that much, the pullbacks are going to be more severe.
"Moves like this take your breath away," she added.

Consuming and producing countries' depleted inventories, which are hovering near 20-year lows, have been behind coffee futures' sustained five-month run-up. Since the beginning of the year, the July contract has rallied more than 175 percent.

Sparking the selloff, however, was a monthly report from the trading house ED&F Man that coffee stocks in consumer nations stood at 10 million bags in April, up from 8.8 million in March and 1.1 million bags higher than a year ago.
Also dampening sentiment was news that private exporters in Colombia were having a hard time finding buyers for about 300,000 bags of green coffee for shipment in June.

Exporters, who originally offered the coffee to European and Japanese roasters, said there have been no takers for the coffee in North America because it is priced against the expensive July contract in New York.

"Roasters are backing off on June purchases even though the Colombians increased supplies to the U.S. and Canada," said Refco Inc analyst Ann Prendergast. "Nobody wants to touch it at this price and they're saying, 'I don't have to buy.'"
Traders said that even with the selloff on Friday, any news of freezing temperatures in the coffee regions of top grower Brazil in June could send prices higher again.
At the New York Mercantile Exchange, heavy selling in palladium futures keyed a fall in precious metals.
Palladium for June delivery closed down $20.90 an ounce at $172.35, while July platinum closed down $9.10 an ounce at $401.20.

"The news about the Russians resuming platinum group metals exports again soon has been making the market nervous. Liquidation of June palladium long positions was also a factor," said Scott Meyers, senior analyst with Pioneer Futures in New York.

Russia's metal export agency, Almaz, said on Thursday that Russia's platinum and palladium exports would resume in the next few weeks. Japanese and Russian officials were expected to meet again early in June to discuss a new metals supply contract.
Japan is one of the biggest consumers of palladium, and Russia supplied 4.6 million ounces of the world's consumption of 6.8 million ounces in 1996.
But fiscal and administrative problems have halted Russian exports since last December, forcing a run on world stocks and a surge in the palladium price to 17-year highs.
Pressured by the selloff in the platinum group, August gold at the COMEX ended down $1.10 at $347.50 an ounce and July silver down 16.3 cents at $4.675 an ounce.
"With gold and silver struggling a little of late, it was not too surprising that they weakened when the white metals sold off sharply today," Meyers said.

At the Chicago Board of Trade, soybean prices closed sharply higher after a weekly report showed much stronger than expected demand from processors last week. Soybeans for July delivery closed 11 cents a bushel higher at $8.80-1/2.
The National Oilseed Processors Association said members crushed 25.462 million bushels of soybeans in the week ended Wednesday, above trade expectations for 23 to 23.7 million.

"Thirty-one million bushels this week in crush and export is far too much to ensure we have sufficient ending stocks," said Joel Karlin, analyst with Everen Securities. "Even with these high prices there continues to be very strong demand."
The crush number added to concerns that supplies of soybeans won't last until the new harvest this fall.
Oil prices closed quietly lower as traders took profits in featureless trading ahead of the weekend.

Crude oil for July delivery on the New York Mercantile Exchange closed 9 cents lower at $20.88 a barrel. July unleaded gasoline fell 0.44 cent to close at 62.81 cents a gallon and July heating oil ended 0.18 cent lower at 55.84 cents.

Traders said the market was waiting to see if a United Nations deal with Iraq that allows it to sell limited amounts of oil to buy food and medicines would be renewed. The current six-month deal expires on June 7.
